title: UML & Architecture Documentation
description: UML and architecture diagrams were a standard engineering communication tool throughout my work at Essential Skills and Square Particle. I used them to design systems, map execution and event flow, reverse-engineer unfamiliar code, plan refactors, debug complex interactions, document architecture, teach new developers, and create shared visual models that teams could understand quickly. For large production systems such as Hydra-Gen, I often created multiple complementary diagrams of the same architecture so each view could focus on a specific concern without overloading a single diagram.

sections.title: Architecture as Visual Communication
paragraphs: I treated UML primarily as a shared visual language for real engineering work rather than as an academic documentation exercise.
The goal was to make architecture, relationships and runtime behavior understandable at a glance to the people designing, maintaining and extending the software.

sections.title: Standard Team Practice
paragraphs: Architecture diagrams were a normal part of development across both Essential Skills and Square Particle.
Over the years my teams and I created hundreds of diagrams using whatever medium best fit the discussion, including paper, whiteboards, Visio, Photoshop and Lucidchart.

sections.title: UML Training & Practical Use
paragraphs: I completed a week-long UML course through Sun Microsystems.

In practice, I followed established UML conventions where they improved shared understanding, but the diagrams were optimized for the team and the engineering question being solved rather than for notation compliance alone.

sections.title: Designed for Rapid Comprehension
paragraphs: I often arranged diagrams spatially to make important relationships visible without requiring the reader to trace a long procedural path.

For event-driven systems, for example, I would place the dispatcher or central system at the visual center so inputs, listeners, outputs and their relative distance from the dispatcher could be understood immediately.

sections.title: Multiple Views for Complex Systems
paragraphs: For large production platforms such as Hydra-Gen, I was more formal in the sense that I created multiple diagrams of the same architecture from different perspectives.
Rather than forcing class structure, runtime flow, persistence, construction, authoring and event relationships into one diagram, each view focused on the concern it needed to explain.

sections.title: Team Communication & Mentoring
paragraphs: The diagrams were consumed by developers, managers, contractors and new hires with a wide range of experience levels.
I used them regularly to explain unfamiliar systems, teach new developers how the architecture worked, and create a common model before implementation or refactoring.

sections.title: 3DForge Weapon-System Refactor
paragraphs: One portfolio example documents my reverse engineering of 3DForge's weapon-firing architecture.
The original implementation used a singleton-based firing system and treated beam and projectile weapons through separate paths, which made supporting multiple independent weapons difficult.

sections.title: Refactoring from the Diagram
paragraphs: I first mapped the existing beam and projectile flows visually, then designed the replacement architecture in a third diagram.

The refactor removed the singleton bottleneck and introduced a common weapon-firing abstraction so beam and projectile implementations could be treated as weapons and instantiated independently at runtime.

sections.title: Customer Operations Architecture
paragraphs: The large AngularJS architecture diagram shown in the portfolio documents the Customer Operations, Sales & Usage Analytics Platform.
It was used to map the relationships across the application's AngularJS, service, data and operational layers.

sections.title: Kingdom Earth Event-Driven Flow
paragraphs: The 'Move Player One Space' diagram came from an unfinished RPG prototype called Kingdom Earth built on MicroGen/C.E.L.L.
It maps player input, movement, event dispatch, listeners, map logic, state persistence and navigation outcomes around the engine's event dispatcher.

sections.title: Influence on C.E.L.L.
paragraphs: During Kingdom Earth development, one collaborator strongly preferred an event-driven architecture.
That work led me to add an Event Dispatcher into C.E.L.L., making event-based coordination available as a reusable engine capability.
